books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”
Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, B. Cotton, Slavery, and the Southern Exception

stimulus.text: A summary of the 1840 census: about one in three white families in the slave states owned enslaved people. In South Carolina, nearly half of white families owned slaves. Most slaveholders owned few enslaved people: about half held fewer than five, and nearly nine in ten held fewer than twenty. Only a small number held more than one hundred.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the 1840 census: about one in three white families in the slave states owned enslaved people, South Carolina 48%, and the distribution of holdings from the census returns. Checked against Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A, which states that the majority of white Southerners owned no slaves.

source: original; data summary from the 1840 United States census
stem: Most white Southern families owned no slaves, yet slavery defined Southern society. Which explanation best fits the figures?

options.text: Slavery mattered only to the few families who owned slaves
options.misconception: If slavery mattered only to owners, it could not have defined a society where most owned none.

options.text: Non-slaveholders were forbidden by law from supporting slavery
options.misconception: No law forbade non-slaveholders from supporting slavery; most supported it freely.

options.text: Slavery shaped the whole region's economy, politics, and racial order
Most white Southerners worked as overseers on large plantations
options.misconception: Most non-slaveholders were small farmers, not overseers on large plantations.

rationales.A: If slavery mattered only to owners, it could not have defined a society where most owned none.
rationales.B: No law forbade non-slaveholders from supporting slavery. Most supported it freely.
rationales.C: Even families without slaves lived in an economy built on cotton, a politics that defended slavery, and a racial order that put them above Black people.
rationales.D: Most non-slaveholders were small farmers, not overseers on large plantations.
rationales.general:
1. Read the figures. About seven in ten white families owned no slaves, yet slavery defined the South.
2. Ask what reaches beyond owners. Cotton set prices and credit, politics defended slavery, and white supremacy ordered daily life.
3. Name the answer. Slavery was not a private possession; it was the region's whole system.
Background: Barron's notes that most white Southerners owned no slaves, yet slavery was seen as essential to the Southern way of life.
Remember: an institution can rule a society even when most people do not own a share of it.
